stem: One point is $({=kx}, {=ky})$. A second point's {=missingCoord}-coordinate is unknown; its other coordinate is ${=otherVal}$. The distance between the two points is ${=distance}$ units{=restrictionNote}. Mark every value the missing coordinate could be.
solution: Write the distance formula: $\text{distance}^2 = (\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2$.
Substitute the known coordinates and the given distance, then isolate the squared difference that holds the missing coordinate.
Take the square root of both sides, keeping both the positive and the negative root.
Add each root to the known coordinate to get the two candidate values, then drop any candidate a stated restriction rules out.
Mark every value that survives on the number line.
notes: Reframes the algebra (solve for the missing coordinate given a distance) as marking the resulting solution set on a number line, which is a genuine fit because this LO's own difficulty IS root multiplicity, not plotting. Rows 1-3 mirror ex8-2-6a, ex8-2-6b and ex8-2-7 exactly (two valid values each); row 4 is an authored analogue of ex8-6-33b's pattern (a stated restriction eliminates one algebraic root), using clean 3-4-5 numbers rather than ex8-6-33b's own figures/quadrilateral context since that question is embedded in a multi-part figure problem. missed-values fires whenever a student reports only one root (stops-at-first-root) and is the likelier error since three of four rows have no restriction to forget; extra-values fires when the eliminated root is marked anyway (keeps-both-roots-ignores-restriction), which only row 4 can trigger. Deliberately leaves out a predicate for the LO1 sign-drop misconception (drops-double-negative-sign): the mapping from 'sign-flipped' (a value marked as its own negative) to a lost sign inside a $(a-(-b))$ subtraction was not clean enough to assert with confidence, so it is omitted rather than forced.
